vignette:
# A Stranger in His Own Life

Marco sits in the leather chair across from me with the posture of someone accustomed to standing at attention, though his hands betray him—they rest in his lap, fingers interlaced so tightly the knuckles have gone white. He's a retired Navy officer, fifty-five, with salt-and-pepper hair and the kind of weathered face that comes from decades of sun exposure on the water. Yet there's something else in his face now: a wariness, as though he's perpetually scanning for threats.

He tells me about the assignment. Twenty-three years in the Navy had taken him all over the world, but the deployment to assess humanitarian operations in the coastal region felt different. It was supposed to be administrative work—evaluating naval support for civilian relief efforts during an ongoing conflict. His partner, Elena, had worried, but Marco had reassured her. He was an officer, not combat personnel. He would be safe.

The morning of the incident, Marco was driving to the coordination center with two local staff members. He was navigating through the city's main thoroughfare when the world simply exploded. A vehicle detonated near theirs. He remembers the sound first—not the boom he might have imagined, but something more primal, a force that compressed his chest and shattered the windows. He remembers the smell: smoke, burning metal, something else he still cannot name. He remembers the silence after, which was somehow worse than the noise.

Marco sustained minor injuries—a concussion, lacerations—but the two local staff members died. He was extracted by military personnel and eventually medically cleared to return home. The official report called it an accident. A fuel truck, they said. An accident.

But that's not what Marco sees when he closes his eyes.

He returned to his apartment in San Diego where Elena waited. She says she felt him disappear before he actually left. He moved through their home like a ghost, sleeping in fragments, waking in the early hours before dawn. When she touched him unexpectedly, he would flinch violently. Once, she came around the corner while he was in the kitchen, and he nearly struck her—his body responding before his mind could catch up.

The sounds are the worst part. He's become hypervigilant to a degree that embarrasses him. A car backfiring on the street sends him diving behind the couch. The Fourth of July fireworks last summer nearly hospitalized him. He sits in restaurants with his back to the wall, always scanning exits. Elena has learned not to approach him from behind.

His career had given him identity and purpose. Now, even the thought of returning to his office at the naval base triggers a suffocating anxiety. He's taken medical leave, but he feels like an imposter—a Navy officer afraid of loud noises, unable to trust his own reactions. The man who trained others in crisis management cannot manage his own mind.

What troubles him most is the guilt. He survived. The two young men who were simply doing their jobs did not. He replays the moments constantly, searching for what he could have done differently, though intellectually he knows there was nothing. Elena finds him some mornings standing in the shower, fully clothed, unable to remember how he got there.

He tells me all of this in measured tones, the way a man trained in discipline speaks about failure. But his hands remain clenched, and when a siren passes outside my office building, he goes absolutely still.
